newsitem.title: USA: NASA signs $7 billion shuttle pact.
newsitem.headline: NASA signs $7 billion shuttle pact.

text.p: The U.S. space agency said on Monday it had signed a $7 billion deal to place the day-to-day running of the shuttle programme in private hands.

The United Space Alliance (USA), a Houston-based joint venture of Rockwell International Corp and Lockheed Martin Corp., signed the contract with NASA last Thursday, said Tommy Holloway, the agency's shuttle programme manager.

"This is a very, very major turning point for this agency," said NASA administrator Daniel Goldin. "What we are saying today is NASA believes in our very strong aerospace companies; they're going to do a job that will cause the shuttle to operate safer (and) ... for much less money."

Under the initial six-year agreement, the alliance will become the single prime contractor for shuttle operations, with responsibility for preparing the fleet of four spaceships for launch, training astronauts and operating mission control.

United Space Alliance was formed in August 1995 by Rockwell and Lockheed Martin to bid on the contract with NASA. As part of Boeing's acquisition of Rockwell's aerospace and defence business, Rockwell's share of the alliance will be transferred to a unit of Boeing, pending approvals later this year, the venture said in a statement.
NASA will retain overall control of the shuttle programme and will adopt a safety oversight role similar to that of Federal Aviation Administration.
Most of the work is performed at the agency's launch site at Cape Canaveral, Florida, and at the Johnson Space Centre, Texas, the home of mission control.
The contract could eventually consolidate more than 85 shuttle contracts, but initially covers just 12, all of which were already held by the two companies forming the partnership.

The next phase of the privatisation would bring another 16 contracts under the control of USA, covering the supply of critical shuttle components such as the liquid-fuelled main engines, external fuel tanks and solid rocket boosters.
The contract includes two, two-year extension options that could boost the value of the deal to $12 billion over 10 years.
The goal of the pact is to cut shuttle operating costs by at least $400 million over six years, said USA spokesman Barbara Zelon.

"There is not a guaranteed number in the sense of a fixed price," said Kent Black, chief executive officer of USA. "We have arrived at a contract that motivates us to save safety first, then meet the manifest, then reduce costs. In that order."

Once the $400 million cost reductions are achieved, the contract includes incentives that allow USA to retain 35 percent of any additional savings. There are also cash penalties for missed schedule targets and if safety levels fall below what NASA considers to be "very good."

An independent safety panel warned earlier this year that NASA needed to slow its privatisation effort or risk an accident. The White House also ordered an independent safety review into the move to a single contractor.

"I know people are very, very nervous about this because change is also difficult," said Goldin. "The fact of the matter is we routinely fly on airliners ... because the government (validates) ... it's safe to fly."
The first shuttle launch under the new pact is scheduled for November 8.
